video_title: On Inflation, Capital Spending & Economic Resilience
gist: Ed Yardeni (Sept 28 webinar) stays in 'proceed with caution' mode as the 10-year Treasury hits ~5.25% in a globally synchronized bond rout driven by Middle East oil risk, strong growth, AI bond and deficit supply, and a possible yen carry trade unwind. He says the rise is in real (TIPS) yields rather than inflation expectations, that a rate-insensitive economy with record forward earnings can withstand current levels, but that 6% or a faster move would threaten the economy and P/E multiples.

insights.claim: The US 10-year Treasury yield has climbed to about 5.25-5.26% in what Yardeni calls an unrelenting, globally synchronized bond rout, with 2-year yields also rising.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Long-duration assets face a rate regime well above the 4-5% range Yardeni previously considered normal.
insights.quote: this has been a pretty unrelenting uh route in in the bond market

insights.claim: Yardeni lists the drivers of higher yields as: re-escalation of the Middle East war lifting oil (stickier inflation, more central bank hikes), a robust US and global economy, more AI-related bond issuance, a roughly $2 trillion federal deficit, and a possible yen carry trade unwind.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Multiple non-cyclical supply and policy forces mean yields may not quickly mean-revert.

insights.claim: Unlike past cycles where deficits widened in recessions while private credit demand was weak, today's ~$2 trillion deficit coincides with an economy growing around 5% in Q3, so Treasury supply is now pushing yields higher.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Bond supply/demand, historically a minor driver, now matters - bearish for duration while deficits stay large in expansion.

insights.claim: Yardeni previously believed the 10-year had normalized in a 4-5% range like the pre-GFC years, but structural changes have pushed it above 5%.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: His anchor range for yields has broken, raising the floor for discount rates.

insights.claim: Yardeni says he will start worrying about rates hurting the US economy if the 10-year reaches 6%, or sooner if the move accelerates, because speed matters as much as level.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: 6% on the 10-year is a key line for a shift from cautious to bearish on the economy.
insights.quote: I'll start worrying about this having an negative impact on the economy if we get up to to six

insights.claim: The rise in Treasury yields since the start of the year and the Middle East war has been driven by TIPS real yields, while the 10-year breakeven spread has stayed flat around 2-2.5%, so it is not an inflation-expectations problem.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Rising real yields point to a higher neutral rate and stronger growth, not runaway inflation - shapes positioning in TIPS vs nominals.
insights.quote: so it's not it's not an inflation problem, believe it or not

insights.claim: Yardeni suspects bond-market algorithms and 'whales' are driving yields higher and amplifying downside volatility in bond prices, for example shorting bonds immediately after the stronger-than-expected September 23 S&P Global PMI release.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Market structure can overshoot fundamentals; data surprises may trigger outsized yield spikes.

insights.claim: Asked whether a rapid rise in rates risks a crash like 1987, Yardeni answered yes, saying more credibility must now be given to debt-crisis scenarios from Ray Dalio and Jim Grant.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A top strategist openly acknowledging crash risk from rate velocity is a tail-risk signal for hedging.

insights.claim: Yardeni frames the bond rout as possibly the price paid for abnormal monetary policy from the Great Financial Crisis through the pandemic, with ultra-low Japanese rates for decades enabling carry trades into foreign government bonds and larger deficits.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If the rout reflects unwinding of decade-long distortions, it may be persistent rather than cyclical.

themes.theme: Global tightening cycle and yen carry unwind

insights.claim: Most major central banks have hiked at least once this year, and 2-year yields across major countries signal further hikes are needed, driven by higher-for-longer oil prices and better-than-expected economies.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A synchronized global tightening cycle raises the risk something breaks in credit markets.

insights.claim: Yardeni treats 2-year government yields as a reliable indicator of where central banks must move policy rates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A simple tool to front-run policy moves across countries.

insights.claim: Rising Japanese yields appear to be leading global bond yields higher, which Yardeni attributes to a possible yen carry trade unwind driven by higher Japanese funding costs, not just yen moves.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Carry trade unwinds can transmit Japanese tightening into US and global bond yields simultaneously.

insights.claim: The Japanese 2-year yield versus the Bank of Japan policy rate implies at least two, possibly three, more BOJ rate hikes.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Further BOJ hikes raise carry funding costs and pressure global duration.

insights.claim: Yardeni sees no viable replacement for the yen as a carry-trade funding currency because it requires a liquid money and bank loan market, and investors will not go to China.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Without a substitute funding source, a yen carry unwind removes demand for foreign bonds rather than relocating it.

insights.claim: China is the only major market where bond yields have been falling this year.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: China bonds are diverging from the global rout - a potential diversifier.

insights.claim: Germany is doing surprisingly well thanks to AI and defense spending despite its auto industry struggling against China, keeping pressure on the ECB to keep raising rates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: German defense and AI capex is a growth source that keeps European rates elevated.

insights.claim: The US economy is less interest-rate sensitive partly because about 30% of US households are headed by someone 65 or older, and many seniors benefit from higher rates via money market funds and bank deposits.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Higher rates may boost rather than squeeze a large spending cohort, delaying any rate-induced slowdown.
insights.quote: 30% of households in America now are headed by somebody 65 years old or older

insights.claim: Housing has been in a recession for some time due to high mortgage rates, the clearest example of a K-shaped economy, but consumer spending has more than offset it.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Housing-linked equities remain under pressure while consumer-facing names hold up.

insights.claim: Capital spending remains strong and much of it is committed to finishing projects already underway, so it continues even if higher rates make some new projects uneconomic.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Capex momentum gives a lag before rates bite - supportive for capex suppliers near term.

insights.claim: Nominal US GDP grew 6.6% in Q2 and may reach around 7% in Q3; under the bond vigilante model, yields must exceed nominal GDP growth to really slow the economy, so 5.25% is unlikely to take it down.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: With yields still below nominal growth, recession risk from current rates looks limited.

insights.claim: The Atlanta Fed GDPNow model was showing about 5.1% real growth, Yardeni's preferred short-term GDP gauge.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Very strong real growth argues against near-term recession and for more tightening.

insights.claim: Global industrial production and exports dipped during the Middle East war but are back near record highs, and MSCI All Country World revenues per share are accelerating broadly across regions, possibly helped by worldwide AI spending.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Global resilience supports earnings, but also removes any reason for central banks to stop hiking.

insights.claim: Because the economy is less rate-sensitive, the neutral real rate is likely higher than the Fed assumed; Kevin Walsh (as named in the transcript) described the recent quarter-point hike as merely removing accommodation, implying more to remove.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A Fed that sees itself as still accommodative implies more hikes than markets priced earlier in the year.

insights.claim: Yardeni expects the core PCE deflator to rise about 0.27% month-over-month, in line with the Cleveland Fed nowcast, with year-over-year PCE inflation staying above 3%.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Sticky 3%-handle inflation keeps pressure on the Fed to tighten further.

insights.claim: Bringing yields down requires lower oil prices, which Yardeni thinks is less likely after Trump warned Iran he would resume bombing absent a deal, while Iran offers reopening the strait in exchange for ending the blockade.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Geopolitical deadlock keeps an oil risk premium embedded in inflation and yields.

insights.claim: Forward earnings are at all-time highs for large caps and SMID caps and analysts unusually raised estimates ahead of earnings season, but much of the year-to-date gain in forward earnings has been offset by a falling forward P/E.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Equity returns hinge on multiple stability; earnings are not the problem.

insights.claim: Yardeni argues P/E compression so far reflects investors failing to chase exceptional earnings rather than recession fears, but real trouble comes if rising rates make investors fear recession and cut multiples further.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Watch for recession talk tied to 6% yields as the trigger for a sharper derating.

insights.claim: With analysts expecting about $418 per share in forward S&P 500 earnings for next year, an 18-20 multiple implies roughly 7,900-8,400 for the index, with risk of a lower P/E if the bond market spooks investors.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete valuation range for the index under current earnings expectations.

insights.claim: Investors are retreating into the Magnificent 7, which caught fire after July helped by Meta's Muse LLM, while the equal-weight S&P 500 underperforms and nears its 200-day moving average.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Narrowing leadership is a defensive signal beneath record Nasdaq highs.

insights.claim: Yardeni rejects the old view that megacaps are rate-insensitive, arguing they are now rate-sensitive because they borrow in bond markets to fund data centers.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Megacap hyperscalers' financing costs rise with yields - a risk the market is overlooking by crowding in.
insights.quote: what's new is that they are sensitive to interest rates because they're borrowing money uh in in the bond market for their data centers

insights.claim: Yardeni expects the Russell 2000, very sensitive to rate-driven recession fears, to break below its 200-day moving average this week.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Small caps are the likely first casualty of rising yields.

insights.claim: US and rest-of-world equity ETFs have moved in lockstep, so the go-global versus stay-home decision has not mattered much this year.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Regional allocation offers little diversification while the driver is a global rate shock.

insights.claim: Yardeni remains in 'proceed with caution' mode, adopted September 15 when the Middle East war looked to be re-escalating, and warns of a volatile week ahead.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A normally bullish strategist staying cautious signals elevated near-term downside risk.
